title: Eval & Quality Monitoring Demo - Polaris AI
summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Polaris AI through the Eval and Quality Monitoring features: building and managing prompt sets, configuring regression alerts, running A/B comparisons, and using the Console + Optimize recommendations. Customer asked about data residency, SOC2 scope, and private deployment options. Agreed next steps: send pricing and security pack, run a short pilot eval with Polaris dataset, schedule benchmark run week of 2025-12-15.

transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-12-03
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Rafael (Redwood Product), Olivia (Polaris Head of ML), Marcus (Eng Mgr), Sana (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy): Demo of Redwood Eval/Quality Monitoring; walked through prompt sets, regression alerts, A/B comparisons; security questions around SOC2/KMS/VPC; agreed pilot and pricing follow-up.

00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a 30-45 min session, quick intros - I'm Maya, AE at Redwood, Jordan our SE will run the demo, Rafael can jump in on product questions.
00:10 Olivia: Hi, Olivia here, head of ML at Polaris, we run recommendation models and have a microsurvey NLU pipeline, curious about monitoring regressions when we reroll models.
00:18 Marcus: Marcus, eng manager, responsible for infra and benchmarks.
00:22 Sana: Sana, security lead, I'll be focused on compliance questions.
00:25 Jordan: Great, quick agenda: overview of Eval in the Console, prompt set management, how to trigger regression alerts, A/B compare flows, and then a short walkthrough of Optimize recommendations for batching and quantization. We'll also show API examples.
00:40 Jordan: So first screen, this is the Eval dashboard - you can see prompt sets on the left, each set has metadata (who created it, baseline model, last run). Note: transcription might say 'Eval board' sometimes in export.
01:05 Marcus: When you say prompt set, is that stored in our account or on Redwood side?
01:12 Jordan: Prompt sets live in the customer's workspace. We persist them encrypted at rest; you can version them. For Private, the control plane sits in Redwood but data plane can be in your VPC — Rafael can confirm.
01:30 Rafael: Yep, for Private deployments the eval artifacts can be configured to store in customer-managed S3 and logs forward to your SIEM, so data residency is controllable.
01:45 Sana: Is that compatible with our KMS? We use AWS KMS with custom policies.
01:50 Rafael: Yes, we integrate with customer KMS, keys can be customer-owned. There's an RBAC layer in the Console for who can run evals or access prompt sets.
02:10 Jordan: Back to the demo - here's a prompt set for our sample ecomm use case. It contains 150 prompts with labels and expected metrics: we compute n-gram accuracy, semantic similarity, and a custom scoring function. You can upload via CSV or use the API.
02:35 Olivia: Can you show how to define an expected output? Our labels are often fuzzy, e.g., sentiment buckets.
02:42 Jordan: Sure - you can set tolerant matching rules, define canonical outputs, or plug in a custom comparator function. The Console shows diff highlights when a candidate deviates.
03:05 Jordan: Now running a baseline against model A (open model variant). This run takes a minute or two depending on prompt count — the Console streams progress.
03:30 (background typing / screen share)
04:05 Jordan: Results - you get per-prompt scores, aggregate metrics, and flagged regressions. The regression alerting system has rules: absolute threshold, percent delta relative to baseline, and a rolling window to avoid noisy flips.
04:40 Marcus: So if we push model B, can we set an alert only for the top-5 intents we care about? We don't want noise from long-tail prompts.
04:50 Jordan: Yep, you can scope alerts to prompt tags or intent groups; our tagging system is part of prompt set metadata. You can also set A/B compare only on a subset.
05:10 Olivia: How do A/B comparisons work in the Console?
05:15 Jordan: We have an A/B compare flow - pick baseline, pick candidate(s), choose the prompt set or subset, then select metrics and significance test (bootstrap/paired t-test). The UI surfaces a wins/losses table and shows examples of prompts that switched label.
05:45 Marcus: Does the system do automatic rollback or traffic split suggestions?
05:50 Jordan: We don't auto-rollback at the moment, but Optimize gives a recommended routing policy: percent traffic, warming, and compatibility with quantized variants. You can export a rollout config for Dedicated/Dedicated pools.
06:10 Olivia: Example: we saw a 3% drop in recall for our entity extraction after quantizing. Can Redwood detect that automatically?
06:20 Jordan: Yes, if you include your eval prompt set for entity extraction and set the metric to recall, a regression alert will trigger if the delta exceeds your set threshold, and we can tag the alert with the model variant (quantized int8 v int16).
06:45 Sana: On security: are raw prompts or model outputs stored? What's retention?
06:52 Rafael: By default, eval inputs/outputs are retained for 90 days; for Private we can align retention to your policy and configure S3 lifecycle rules. There's an option to redact PII on ingest or encrypt with your KMS.
07:10 Sana: Do you have SOC2 and pen test reports?
07:14 Maya: Yes we have SOC2 Type II and recent penetration test summary - we'll share the security pack after this call. Action: Maya to send to Sana.
07:30 Jordan: Demo continued - here's a sample alert timeline. You can configure escalation: email, Slack, webhook to your incident system. Alerts include sample prompts that triggered the regression so your team can triage quickly.
08:00 Marcus: How noisy are these alerts in practice? If we run daily evals we might get too many false positives.
08:07 Jordan: We provide noise controls: rolling windows, minimum sample counts, and you can require consistent failure across multiple runs before firing. Also you can set severity buckets so only major regressions notify on-call.
08:30 Olivia: For A/B we'll want to see human review diffs. Can we attach annotator feedback?
08:36 Jordan: Yes, human-in-the-loop: reviewers can annotate examples, and those annotations become part of the prompt set for future evals. You can also integrate with your annotation store via webhook.
09:05 (brief cross-talk)
09:20 Jordan: Now API examples — here's how to call the Eval API to run a prompt set programmatically. The endpoint accepts a JSONL of prompts and the comparator; it returns per-prompt scores and a run_id.
09:40 Marcus: Do you stream outputs back or is it batch?
09:45 Jordan: Eval runs are batch, we stream progress. For single-prompt live checks you can use the Redwood API generation with a scoring comparator locally.
10:05 Jordan: Switching to Optimize: this suggests batching, kv cache settings, and quantization profile per workload. For the ecomm prompt set it suggested dynamic batch size 8 with max latency SLO 250ms and mixed-int8 profile.
10:35 Olivia: Is that recommendation evidence-based? Like it runs a small benchmark?
10:40 Jordan: Yes Optimize runs short microbenchmarks on representative prompt lengths and shows expected cost/latency tradeoffs. There's a confidence score.
11:00 (silence / typing)
11:20 Sana: Quick question about private deployment: if we run Private in our VPC, can we still use the Console hosted by Redwood?
11:28 Rafael: We offer both — a private control plane (so Console is in your VPC) or a hybrid where control plane metadata is in Redwood but artifacts live in your S3. For strict compliance we do fully private control plane and on-prem if needed.
11:50 Sana: And audit logs?
11:54 Rafael: Audit logs are available and can be forwarded to your CloudWatch or Splunk. They include run_ids, who triggered evals, and changes to prompt sets.
12:20 Marcus: For the pilot, we'd like Redwood to run our 500-prompt set against two model variants and produce a report with top 50 failing prompts. Can you do that?
12:30 Maya: Absolutely, Jordan will run the eval as part of the pilot. We'll need the prompt set and expected outputs. Marcus: we'll share by Friday.
12:42 Jordan: Note: our scorer supports custom comparator functions — if you have a fuzzy matcher we can incorporate it in the pilot.
13:05 Olivia: How do you handle ground truth that is multi-label? For example an utterance could map to multiple intents.
13:12 Jordan: We support multi-label ground truth; metrics include set-based precision/recall and you can weight labels. The Console shows confusion matrices.
13:40 (short pause)
13:55 Jordan: Walkthrough of alert config UI — show rule creation: metric (e.g., exact match, semantic sim), threshold, scope (tags), rolling window (3 runs), and webhook destinations. You can test the rule against historical runs.
14:20 Marcus: Can we export results to our data warehouse?
14:25 Jordan: Yes exports via CSV, JSONL, and direct connector to BigQuery/Snowflake (for Dedicated/Private or via secure transfer).
14:45 Olivia: Any pricing notes for eval runs? We don't want cost surprises running nightly checks.
14:52 Maya: Eval runs are priced by compute minutes and prompt count; for Dedicated customers there's a discounted rate. We'll send an infra & pricing deck with examples.
15:10 Sana: One more on encryption: do you encrypt outputs in transit?
15:15 Rafael: All traffic is TLS 1.2+; for Private customers we can require mTLS between agents.
15:30 (demo winding down)
15:45 Jordan: Quick recap: we showed prompt set creation, baseline runs, regression alerts, A/B compare flow, and Optimize recommendations.
15:55 Maya: Next steps: Maya to share pricing and security pack, Jordan to share sample eval notebook and run pilot with Polaris dataset, Marcus to schedule pilot week of 2025-12-15.
16:10 Olivia: Sounds good. Marcus and I will prepare the prompt set and expected outputs and send to Jordan.
16:20 Sana: I'll send SOC2 scope Qs and legal contact.
16:30 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and notes.

Transcript notes: transcription has occasional errors (product names sometimes mis-transcribed, e.g., "Optimise" vs "Optimize", "KV cache" sometimes "K-V cash"). There is natural crosstalk and filler. References shared: pricing deck (link: https://redwood.example/decks/pricing), security pack (link: https://redwood.example/security-pack.pdf), eval notebook template (link: https://redwood.example/templates/eval-notebook.ipynb).
